meta.title: aliro.mayday — your door key lives in your phone
meta.description: An experimental Aliro NFC controller on ESP32-S3 + PN532. Public source and wiring diagrams, a working iPhone key, and current Samsung testing status.

hero.title: Your door key lives in your phone
hero.lede: An experimental NFC controller built on ESP32-S3 and PN532. An existing iPhone key works on the bench; Samsung Wallet through SmartThings is being prepared for testing. Source code and wiring diagrams are public.

why.title: Why this beats a dedicated app

1.title: Already on your phone
1.text: The tested iPhone path uses an Apple Wallet key. Issuance into other wallets still needs testing.

2.title: Hardware-level security
2.text: The reader checks phone signatures, key binding and access permissions. Security of the complete installation requires a separate audit and hardware tests.

3.title: Works offline
3.text: NFC communication is directly with the phone. Document-based access requires a valid clock; prolonged network-loss behaviour still needs testing.

4.title: One open standard
4.text: Aliro 1.0 defines common access protocols. The project implements an NFC subset; provisioned keys and rules determine which readers permit access.

why.lede: We use the open Aliro standard and publish the prototype code. Wallet compatibility is established by testing, not by the standard name alone.

migration.title: Gradual migration, no big-bang switch
migration.lede: A gradual move from cards to digital keys remains a planned use case. The current Aliro firmware is not a complete office migration system.

1.title: Install the controller
1.text: First verify controller wiring and the existing access method. Preserving working access is a requirement for a future migration.

2.title: Import the card database
2.text: PM3 tools for UID research are included separately. Bulk card import, employee permissions and a working access-control database are not implemented in the Aliro firmware.

3.title: Migrate one at a time
3.text: Digital-key provisioning and revocation use Matter. Joint operation of iPhone, Samsung and existing cards still requires separate tests.

migration.formats: PN532 is used over SPI for Aliro NFC. Chip support for a card family does not establish working access credentials for that family in this project.

standard.title: About the Aliro standard
standard.lede: Aliro 1.0 is the Connectivity Standards Alliance standard for digital access credentials. This project is an experimental implementation of its NFC subset.
standard.timeline_title: How the standard came to be

1.text: Inside the Connectivity Standards Alliance (CSA) — the non-profit IoT-manufacturer alliance — a working group starts on a unified access protocol, building on the proven Apple HomeKey and automotive CCC CarKey approaches.

2.text: On November 9, the CSA publicly announces Aliro. Around 200 member companies are already on board: Apple, Google, Samsung, ASSA ABLOY, Allegion, NXP, Infineon, and others. The stated goal — make the phone a universal key.

3.text: On February 26, Aliro 1.0 ships — a 195-page specification freely available from the CSA site. The ecosystem is now 220+ companies. The first certified locks begin rolling out.

1.title: Asymmetric cryptography
1.text: P-256 signatures authenticate keys. The reader does not receive the phone's private key; protection of that key depends on the wallet platform.

2.title: Secure channel
2.text: Separate directional keys and message counters protect the exchange. Correct validation and an installation security review remain necessary.

3.title: NFC, BLE, and UWB
3.text: Aliro defines NFC, BLE and UWB access paths. This firmware enables NFC access; BLE is used for Matter commissioning, and UWB access is not implemented.

4.title: Cloud-free
4.text: NFC authentication runs locally. Provisioning, credential updates and revocation delivery depend on the selected ecosystem; document-bound access also needs a valid clock.

standard.disclaimer: aliro.mayday implements and tests a documented NFC subset of Aliro 1.0. Full wallet interoperability, BLE/UWB access and certification are not established. The public documentation lists implemented checks, unsupported restrictions and remaining hardware acceptance.

integrations.title: More than a reader — it's a controller
integrations.lede: Matter DoorLock and local web diagnostics are available. Relay control and Telegram notifications are implemented in the shared source and browser demo; physical operation still needs testing.

1.title: Remote control
1.text: Matter commands and authenticated NFC use the same optional relay driver. Telegram has no lock-control commands.

2.title: Real-time alerts
2.text: Lock-state notifications and optional NFC-denial alerts are implemented. Try simulated delivery in the demo; live Telegram delivery still needs testing.

3.title: Video surveillance
3.text: Frigate, UniFi Protect and other NVRs are candidates for event-based integration. No tested camera integration is available yet.

4.title: Attack detection
4.text: Signatures, key binding and access permissions are tested. Complete relay-attack protection, UWB and case-tamper detection are not implemented.

5.title: Analytics and metrics
5.text: Local diagnostic metrics exist. Prometheus export and ready-made Grafana dashboards remain planned.

6.title: Your own ecosystem
6.text: The main path is Matter DoorLock. Google Home and SmartThings/Samsung Wallet still need testing; other examples and patches are included as separate projects.

roadmap.title: Work plan
roadmap.lede: Status on 15 October 2026. Completed stages refer to the prototype; certification and finished-device dates have not been announced.

1.title: Hardware and platform
1.text: ESP32-S3 + PN532 over SPI. Pin diagrams are published; a physical actuator driver is still missing.

2.title: Matter and NFC
2.text: Matter DoorLock, DigitalDoorKey, Standard/Fast, rights validation and key revocation. Persistence and provisioning errors have host coverage.

3.title: Wallet testing
3.text: The existing iPhone key passed the updated-firmware bench test on 15 October: three authenticated taps, zero failures, and lock-state changes in both directions. Samsung Fold 7 through SmartThings remains pending.

4.title: Local administration
4.text: Web diagnostics and logs are available. Complete administration and secure external integrations still need work.

5.title: Cameras and automation
5.text: NVR, Prometheus and Grafana integrations are not verified capabilities.

6.title: Control backend
6.text: Relay control and notification-only Telegram support are implemented in source. Hardware acceptance, cameras, Mini App and long-term analytics remain future work.

7.title: Finished device
7.text: Physical lock output, hardware acceptance, audit, power behaviour and certification are still required.

privacy.title: Your data
privacy.lede: The controller is built local-first. By default, nothing leaves your device. Any outbound integration happens only when you explicitly enable it.

1.title: The key never leaves your phone
1.text: The phone private key is not transferred to the reader. The controller stores its own keys and provisioned credentials; backups of that state must stay private.

2.title: Local access validation
2.text: NFC validation runs on the controller. Wallet key issuance may require an account and service from the selected ecosystem; no project cloud account is required to read the source.

3.title: Event log and alerts stay local
3.text: Web diagnostics run locally. Tested log delivery to Telegram, MQTT and external services is not claimed yet.

4.title: Verifiable architecture
4.text: Source, access-policy and revocation fixes, tests and wiring diagrams are available on GitHub. Main project code has a commercial source-available license; components retain their MIT/ISC and other licenses. Public source is not Aliro certification.

1.q: Do I need internet to unlock the door?
1.a: NFC communication is directly with the phone. Document-based access requires a valid controller clock; remote Matter commands require a network. Key issuance depends on the wallet ecosystem. Behaviour during prolonged network loss still needs bench testing.

2.q: What if my phone is dead?
2.a: Depleted-battery behaviour depends on the phone model and provisioned key. It has not been tested on our bench, so no runtime is promised. Keep an independent way to enter the premises.

3.q: I lost my phone — can someone open my door?
3.a: A lost phone requires access revocation. Firmware handles disabled users, removed keys and signed revocation documents. Signed revocation takes effect after delivery to the controller; automatic Find My or Google Find integration is not implemented. Key and biometric behaviour depends on the wallet, including Express Mode.

4.a: The current target is ESP32-S3 + PN532 using the published wiring guide. An optional GPIO relay driver is implemented and disabled by default; physical relay testing is pending. This prototype is not a certified Aliro lock. Check commercial locks with their manufacturer.

5.q: Can someone intercept the NFC signal and open the lock?
5.a: Cryptographic signatures and key permissions are checked. This does not establish complete relay-attack protection. UWB, tamper sensors and tested attack alerts are not part of the current build.

6.a: Source and build instructions are public in ilia-ae/aliro-mayday. Start with the pin diagram and the guide for preserving keys during an update. License v1.1 permits personal non-commercial builds, changes, forks and free redistribution within its scope; commercial use of project-original code requires a separate agreement. A physical actuator driver still needs to be added.

7.a: Yes, under a paid commercial licence. Selling devices, deploying in offices / hotels / commercial buildings, integrating into a paid product, white-label, OEM — all on the table. Pricing is typically per-device, revenue-share, or a flat licence fee, depending on volume and scenario. Write to aliro.mayday@ilia.ae or reach out via ilia.ae to discuss terms.

8.q: If Wi-Fi goes down — does Matter / Telegram break, does the lock stop opening?
8.a: Losing Wi-Fi should not itself unlock the door. NFC validation is local, but document permissions require a valid clock. Booting without a network and recovery of remote functions still require tests.

lock_shopping.title: Lock wiring and shopping list
lock_shopping.intro: Reference bench latch: SparkFun ROB-15324, 12 V DC / 600 mA. Power retracts its 10 mm bolt; removing power extends it. Use a 1-second unlock pulse; this solenoid is not rated for continuous power.
lock_shopping.diagram_alt: DFR0473 relay wiring: GPIO4 to D, separate 5 V module supply and 12 V lock supply switched through COM/NO.
lock_shopping.hardware_note: Reference wiring for a future firmware update. The working controller has not been updated; physical relay operation still needs testing.
lock_shopping.note: Both supplies have EU plugs and centre-positive 5.5 × 2.1 mm outputs. Links show example parts; equivalents can be sourced locally. Prices and stock may change.

lock.name: SparkFun ROB-15324 solenoid latch
lock.detail: 12 V DC, 600 mA; power-to-unlock. Set Unlock pulse to 1000 ms. Rated for 1–10 s activations; do not use Follow logical lock state. Let it cool between trials.

relay.name: DFRobot DFR0473 relay
relay.detail: Mechanical relay with driver; 3.3 V HIGH control. Check that the seller includes the Gravity cable.

supply5.name: Mean Well GST18E05-P1J
supply5.detail: 5 V DC, 3 A supply for the relay module. The reference needs at least 0.5 A.

supply12.name: Mean Well GST25E12-P1J
supply12.detail: 12 V DC, 2.08 A supply for a compatible bench lock, including its inrush.

resistor.name: 10 kΩ, 0.25 W resistor
resistor.detail: R1 between D and GND. One resistor is needed; sold in a pack.

jumpers.name: Dupont female–female
jumpers.detail: Short signal connections. Use stranded power wire for the lock.

wire.name: 20 AWG stranded copper wire
wire.detail: About 0.5 mm² for short bench power connections; preferably red and black. The linked spool is larger than needed.

adapters.name: DC jack to screw-terminal adapter
adapters.detail: Female 5.5 × 2.1 mm sockets for both supplies, so their plugs can stay intact.

diode.name: 1N4001 suppression diode
diode.detail: For a simple DC coil without built-in suppression, if its instructions allow it. Otherwise use the specified diode/TVS.

1.title: Existing iPhone key verified after firmware update
1.text: The existing iPhone key passed the updated-firmware test without reissuing the key or resetting pairing. The log records three authenticated taps, zero failures and both lock states. HTTP startup and disconnect fixes are published in PR #6; Fold 7 awaits bench acceptance.

2.title: Aliro access controller — positioning shift
2.text: Project scope expanded from "Aliro reader" to "access controller": HTTP API, MQTT, Telegram, CCTV triggers, Prometheus, tamper detection.

3.title: aliro-esp32 skeleton on ESP-IDF + esp-matter
3.text: Firmware scaffold: Matter commissioning over BLE, Wi-Fi transport, NVS persistence. Ready for DoorLock cluster implementation.

4.title: Aliro 1.0 released
4.text: CSA published the final 195-page spec. From that moment, development pivoted from Apple HomeKey to Aliro.

privacy_page.title: Privacy policy
privacy_page.subtitle: Version of April 28, 2026
privacy_page.lede: Short, no legal noise. The aliro.mayday.software site is built to collect a minimum from visitors — ideally zero.

data.title: What data we collect
data.body: Nothing automatic. The site does not load analytics, advertising pixels, or external trackers. There is no cookie banner because there are no cookies.

local.title: What is stored locally in your browser
local.body: Only two settings in localStorage: the chosen theme (light/dark) and language (RU/EN). This data never leaves your device and exists solely so the page renders the same way on your next visit. You can clear it via browser settings at any time.

email.title: Email and inquiries
email.body: If you write to aliro.mayday@ilia.ae we see your address and message. We use this data only to reply to your inquiry. We do not share with third parties, do not subscribe you to mailings, do not add you to marketing databases.

third_parties.title: Third parties
third_parties.body: The site is hosted on Cloudflare Workers — Cloudflare sees technical request data (IP, User-Agent) at the network level like any CDN. Their policy applies separately. Beyond that, no other third-party services are loaded on the site.

controller.title: The controller itself
controller.body: The aliro.mayday controller operates locally and does not send any access-event data anywhere by default. Any integration (MQTT, Telegram, webhooks) is enabled by the owner explicitly — details in the "Your data" section on the homepage.

status.title: What we're building
status.p1: On 15 October 2026, the owner confirmed that the existing iPhone key works after the firmware update. The controller recorded three authenticated taps, zero failures and both locked and unlocked Matter states. The key and pairing were preserved.
status.p2: Automated checks for access rights, revocation and persistence pass. Samsung Wallet on Fold 7, Google Wallet, a physical relay and Aliro BLE/UWB remain unverified.
